claims.text: The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi baseline has dual-phase lamellar colonies.
Unmodified interlamellar boundaries in the baseline alloy serve as microcrack-initiation sites during tensile loading.
Adding 1–2 at.% Ti during melt-casting and homogenizing at approximately 800°C induces Ti segregation to interlamellar boundaries.
The segregated Ti forms a dopant-enriched interfacial complexion.
The Ti-enriched interfacial complexion enhances interfacial bonding and cohesion.
Enhanced interfacial cohesion inhibits or delays microcrack nucleation.
Controlled cooling can retain the Ti-modified interfacial complexion without disrupting the lamellar morphology.
Ti has low solubility in the relevant phases and a strong affinity for the interlamellar boundaries.
Ti segregation reduces microvoid formation during tensile deformation.
Ti can hinder dislocation motion and produce a dispersion-strengthening effect.
The Ti-doped alloy will have greater yield strength than the unmodified baseline.
The Ti-doped alloy will have greater ultimate tensile strength than the unmodified baseline.
The Ti-doped alloy will have greater room-temperature tensile ductility than the unmodified baseline.
Strengthened interfacial bonding delays microcrack propagation.
Excessive or poorly controlled Ti addition and heat treatment can produce unwanted Ti-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The intervention succeeds only if Ti segregation is achieved without deleterious Ti-rich secondary-phase formation and without loss of the dual-phase lamellar structure.
Prior literature supports dopant segregation as a means of improving interfacial cohesion.
